slides.headline:
The last ship out of Hungnam
carried a noodle shop.
slides.subline: Naeho Naengmyeon — open since 1919, and the alley where Busan's milmyeon is said to have been born

slides.label:
The year this family opened
its first noodle shop — in what
is now North Korea
slides.note: Reopened in Busan in March 1953, after the December 1950 Hungnam evacuation · listed among South Korea's oldest still-operating restaurants

items.d: The northern original the family had made since 1919. Both ingredients were scarce and expensive in wartime Busan.
They switched to wheat, which was arriving as American army aid. Springier, chewier, and something refugees could afford.
Other Busan shops dispute the claim, but Naeho is the one most often named as milmyeon's starting point.

slides.title:
A Busan classic
invented by a shortage
slides.body:
The shop opened in 1919 as Dongchun Myeonok, in Naeho-ri near Hungnam. In December 1950 the family boarded the Hungnam evacuation — the sealift South Koreans still call the Miracle of Christmas. The current owner-chef, You Sang-mo, told The Korea Times he was three, riding on his aunt's back on the last ship out.

They reopened in Busan in March 1953 and later renamed the shop Naeho, after the village they could no longer return to. Milmyeon began as a substitution — and became the dish the city is known for.
